subcategory: Responsible AI, Human Rights and Safety
oneSentence: Inclusion means designing and using AI so different people can access it, be represented in it, and avoid being unfairly left out or harmed.
plainExplanation:
In AI, inclusion means asking who can use a system, who is represented in the data, and who may be excluded by design choices. It covers language, disability, internet access, literacy, culture, gender, age, and other factors that affect whether a tool works fairly for real people.

What goes in are design choices, training data, testing plans, and decisions about where and how the system will be used. If those inputs mostly reflect one group, one language, or one kind of device, the system may work well for some people and poorly for others.

What happens is not magic. Teams choose examples, labels, interfaces, rules, and review processes. They test the system with different user groups and contexts, then fix barriers they find. A barrier can be technical, such as poor speech recognition for some accents, or practical, such as a tool that only works with fast internet.

What comes out can be broader access and fewer people left behind. But inclusion is not the same as fairness, accessibility, or non-discrimination, even though it overlaps with all three. Inclusion is the wider practice of making sure affected people are considered, represented, and able to participate, while important human decisions still remain under human responsibility.

everydayAnalogy.title: Translating a short field report for a mixed audience
everydayAnalogy.story: A team receives a short field report in French and wants to share it quickly with colleagues in Nairobi, Bangkok, Bogotá and Geneva. One person first makes an English version using an AI tool, but the draft uses uncommon terms, small text, and a chart image with no caption. The team then revises it: they simplify key phrases, add alt text for the chart, check that place names stayed correct, and prepare a version that also works on a low-bandwidth phone. More colleagues can now use the report without guessing or being left out.

mapping.analogyElement: The first draft that only suits some readers
mapping.aiElement: An AI system built around a narrow set of users or contexts

mapping.analogyElement: Adding alt text and clearer wording
mapping.aiElement: Design changes that improve inclusion for different needs
Testing whether outputs represent people and places accurately
Accounting for access limits such as device, connectivity, or cost

everydayAnalogy.limitation: A translated report is a small document, but AI inclusion applies across the whole system life cycle, including data collection, model training, deployment, monitoring, and complaints processes. Also, making one report easier to use does not by itself show whether the underlying AI performs well across groups or avoids discriminatory effects.

visual.title: How inclusion is built into an AI system
visual.learningObjective: Show that inclusion comes from deliberate design and testing choices, not from adding one feature at the end.
visual.description: A left-to-right five-step diagram. Each step shows one point where people can be included or excluded: scoping, data, design, testing, and use. Read from problem definition to deployment and review. Red warning icons mark common exclusion risks; green check icons mark inclusive actions.

steps.label: 1. Define who is affected
steps.explanation: List the groups who may use the system or be affected by it, including people with less access, different languages, or disabilities.
steps.visualInstruction: Draw a box with diverse person icons around it. Add a warning badge labelled 'some users missing?' and a check badge labelled 'include affected groups'.

steps.label: 2. Check the data
steps.explanation: Review whether the examples, labels, and sources represent those groups well enough for the task.
steps.visualInstruction: Draw a dataset box feeding into the process. Show uneven stacks for under-represented groups, then a corrected balanced set beside it.

steps.label: 3. Design for real conditions
steps.explanation: Build interfaces and workflows that work across devices, literacy levels, languages, and connectivity conditions.
steps.visualInstruction: Show phone, laptop, screen-reader, and low-signal icons under a design box. Add small labels: 'language', 'format', 'bandwidth', 'readability'.

steps.label: 4. Test with different users
steps.explanation: Measure whether performance and usability differ across groups and contexts, then fix problems before wider use.
steps.visualInstruction: Draw a test panel with several user groups and a results table. Highlight one lower score in red, then an arrow to a repaired version.

steps.label: 5. Monitor and allow feedback
steps.explanation: After deployment, track who benefits, who struggles, and how people can report problems and get human review.
steps.visualInstruction: Show an output box leading to a feedback loop with alert, comment, and human-review icons.

visual.interaction: Users can click each step to reveal one example of exclusion risk and one practical inclusion action.
visual.accessibilityDescription: This diagram explains inclusion as a five-step process. First, identify all groups who may use or be affected by the AI system, not just the easiest users to reach. Second, check whether the data represents those groups well enough. Third, design the system for real conditions such as different languages, devices, disabilities, literacy levels, and internet access. Fourth, test performance and usability across groups and repair gaps. Fifth, after deployment, monitor outcomes and provide ways for people to report problems and get human review. The message is that inclusion must be considered from the start and revisited over time.
visual.reducedMotionDescription: A static five-column diagram with numbered boxes, warning markers for exclusion risks, and check markers for inclusive actions. No animation is used; the feedback loop is shown as a simple curved arrow from deployment back to earlier steps.

workedExample.scenario: A public health organisation pilots an AI tool that classifies incoming SMS messages about clinic services into three categories: appointment, medicine stock, or urgent complaint.
workedExample.input: Pilot data: 600 messages in English from urban users and 120 in Swahili from rural users.
process: The team tests the model separately on both language groups instead of only looking at one overall accuracy score.
Results show 91% accuracy on the English messages but 62% on the Swahili messages, with many urgent complaints mislabelled as routine questions.
The team adds more reviewed Swahili examples, revises labels, and changes the interface so uncertain cases go to human staff.
After retesting, the English score stays high and the Swahili score rises to 84%, with urgent complaints more reliably routed for human attention.
workedExample.result: The tool becomes more inclusive because it serves a wider set of users more reliably instead of mainly working for the majority language group.

unWorkplaceExample.scenario: In a country office, a shared inbox receives public messages in several languages about event registration, service access and general enquiries. Staff consider using an AI triage tool to sort messages by topic and urgency.
unWorkplaceExample.relevance: Inclusion matters because the tool must work for people writing in different languages and styles, including those using simple phones or limited connectivity. The office should test whether some groups' messages are misclassified or routinely sent to slower queues.
unWorkplaceExample.caution: Do not paste personal, confidential, protection-sensitive or security-sensitive message content into an unapproved public AI service. Keep human review for messages that could affect rights, access to services, or safeguarding.

whyItMatters:
If inclusion is ignored, an AI system may work smoothly for people who are already easiest to serve and fail others quietly. That can mean missed services, distorted information, extra burdens on staff, and higher risk of unfair treatment.

For a non-specialist, this matters because choices about data, language, interface, and review shape who benefits and who is left out. A tool can look successful on average while still failing a specific group.

In practical terms, inclusion helps organisations ask better questions before deployment: Who is missing from the data? Who cannot use this interface? Who needs human support instead of automation? Those questions improve quality, reduce harm, and support more accountable decisions.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Inclusion just means adding more demographic groups to the training data.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Data representation matters, but inclusion is broader. It also includes language choice, interface design, device and bandwidth limits, disability access, testing methods, feedback channels, and whether people can get human review when needed.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: If a system is accessible, it is automatically inclusive.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Accessibility focuses on whether people with disabilities can use a product or service. Inclusion is wider. A system might meet accessibility needs yet still exclude people because of language, cost, literacy, geography, or poor representation in the data.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: A high overall accuracy score proves the system is inclusive.
commonMisconceptions.correction: An average score can hide large differences between groups. A model may perform well for the majority and poorly for a minority language, accent, region, or user group. Inclusion requires looking at who benefits and who does not.

simpleVsTechnical.simple: Inclusion means making sure an AI system works for different kinds of people and does not leave some groups out by accident.
simpleVsTechnical.technical: In AI practice, inclusion refers to designing, developing, evaluating and governing systems so affected populations are meaningfully considered across the life cycle. This includes representational coverage in data, participatory or consultative design, usability across languages and contexts, accessibility, and evaluation of differential performance and impact across groups. It is related to fairness and non-discrimination, but it is not identical to either. Fairness often focuses on how outcomes are distributed or whether treatment differs unjustifiably. Inclusion focuses more broadly on whether people can access, use, influence, and benefit from the system, and whether deployment conditions systematically exclude some populations. Inclusion can therefore involve technical measures, such as subgroup testing or better data coverage, and non-technical measures, such as human support channels, localisation, procurement requirements, and ongoing monitoring.

keyTakeaway: Inclusion means asking, at every stage, who is being served, who is being missed, and what must change before the system is trusted in practice.

quickCheck.question: Which example best shows inclusion in AI?
options: Using one overall accuracy score because it is simpler to report
Launching the tool in one major language first and assuming others can adapt
Testing the system with different user groups and redesigning it when some groups are left out
Replacing human review so all cases are treated the same way
quickCheck.explanation: Inclusion requires checking who may be excluded and changing the system accordingly. One overall score can hide group-level problems, one-language design can exclude users, and removing human review can worsen harms in sensitive cases.

contested: The general idea is widely accepted, but organisations may define the boundaries differently. Some use 'inclusion' mainly for participation and access, while others also fold in representation, fairness, accessibility or broader equity concerns.
